''Asiorientales'', as Inferred From Morphology and RAD-Seq Data|journal=Frontiers in Plant Science|issn=1664-462X|volume=13|article-number=824158|doi=10.3389/fpls.2022.824158|pmid=35615129 |pmc=9125193 |bibcode=2022FrPS...1324158C |doi-access=free}} }} '''''Cycas revoluta''''' ('''Sotetsu''' [Japanese '''ソテツ'''], '''sago cycad''', '''sago palm''', '''king sago''', '''Japanese sago palm''') is a [[species]] of [[gymnosperm]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Cycadaceae]], [[native plant|native]] to southern Japan including the Ryukyu Islands. It is one of several species used for the production of [[sago]], as well as an ornamental plant. The sago cycad can be distinguished by a thick coat of fibers on its trunk. The sago cycad is sometimes mistakenly thought to be a palm, although the only similarity between the two is that they look similar and both produce seeds. ==Names== [[Cycad]]s are not related to palms ([[Arecaceae]]), superficially similar only in leaf arrangement and that both are [[vascular plant]]s and [[Spermatophyte|seed plants]]. The Latin [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''revoluta'' means "curled back",{{cite book|first = D. |last =Gledhill |title =The Names of Plants|page=329|publisher = Cambridge University Press|date = 2008|isbn = 978-0-521-86645-3}} in reference to the leaves. This is also called kungi (comb) palm in Urdu speaking areas.{{cite book|last=Harrison|first=Lorraine|title=RHS Latin for gardeners |year= 2012 |publisher=Mitchell Beazley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1-84533-731-5|page=224}} == Description == This very symmetrical plant supports a crown of shiny, dark green leaves on a thick shaggy trunk that is typically about {{convert|20|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter, sometimes wider. The trunk is very low to subterranean in young plants, but lengthens above ground with age. It can grow into very old specimens with {{cvt|6|–|7|m}} of trunk; however, the plant is very slow-growing and requires about 50–100 years to achieve this height. Trunks can branch several times, thus producing multiple heads of leaves.Thunberg, Carl Peter. 1782. Verhandelingen uitgegeeven door de hollandse maatschappy der weetenschappen, te Haarlem 20(2): 424, 426–427. The largest cultivated specimen, at the Ryugeji Temple, in Shimizu, [[Japan]] ({{cvt|136|km}} WSW of Tokyo), is {{cvt|8|m}} in height and {{cvt|1.6|m}} thick.{{cite book | last= Weiland |first= G.R. | date= 1906 | title= American Fossil Cycads | location= Washington, D.C. | publisher= Carnegie Institute | page= 34}} [[Image:Sago cycads Keramashoto.png|thumbnail|King sago palm/Sotetsu growing on a cliff in [[Kerama Shotō National Park]].]] [[Image:CycadKingSago.jpg|thumbnail|King sago palm in [[Humble, Texas]].]] The leaves are a deep semiglossy green and about {{convert|50|–|150|cm|in|abbr=on}} long when the plants are of a reproductive age. They grow out into a feather-like rosette to {{convert|1|m|ft|abbr=on}} in diameter. The crowded, stiff, narrow leaflets are {{convert|8|-|18|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and have strongly recurved or revolute edges. The basal leaflets become more like spines. The petiole or stems of the sago cycad are {{convert|6|–|10|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and have small protective barbs.{{citation needed|date=March 2023}} Roots are called ''coralloid'' with an ''[[Anabaena]]'' symbiosis allowing nitrogen fixation.{{cite journal | last1 = Obukowicz | first1 = M. | last2 = Schaller | first2 = M. | last3 = Kennedy | first3 = G.S. | year = 1981 | title = Ultrastructure and phenolic histochemistry of the Cycas revoluta-Anabaena symbiosis | url = | journal = New Phytologist | volume = 87 | issue = 4| pages = 751–759 | doi = 10.1111/j.1469-8137.1981.tb01711.x | bibcode = 1981NewPh..87..751O }} Tannins-rich cells are found on either side of the [[algal]] layer to resist the algal invasion.{{citation needed|date=March 2023}} As with other cycads, it is [[plant sexuality|dioecious]], with the males bearing [[pollen]] cones ([[strobilus]]) and the females bearing groups of [[megasporophyll]]s. Pollination can be done naturally by [[insect]]s or artificially. This plant is also dangerous, due to poison in the seeds to keep the plant safe. == Cultivation and uses == Propagation of ''Cycas revoluta'' is either by [[seed]] or clonally by removal of basal offsets. It is one of the most widely cultivated cycads, grown outdoors in warm temperate and subtropical regions, or under glass in colder areas. It grows best in sandy, well-drained soil, preferably with some organic matter. It needs good drainage or it will rot. It is fairly drought-tolerant and grows well in full sun or outdoor shade, but needs bright light when grown indoors. The leaves can bleach somewhat if moved from indoors to full sun outdoors.{{citation needed|date=March 2023}} [[File:Snow on Cycas revoluta.jpg|thumbnail|Plant covered with [[snow]].]] Of all the cycads, ''C. revoluta'' is the most popular in cultivation. It is seen in almost all [[botanical garden]]s, in both [[temperateness|temperate]] and [[tropics|tropical]] locations. In many areas of the world, it is heavily promoted commercially as a landscape plant. It is also quite popular as a [[bonsai]] plant. First described in the late 18th century, it is tolerant of mild to somewhat cold temperatures, provided the ground is dry. Frost damage can occur at temperatures below −10 °C (14 °F). ''C. revoluta'' usually defoliates in winter in this temperate climate, but will usually flush (grow) several new leaves by spring. This plant has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]{{cite web|title=''Cycas revoluta''|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/5127/Cycas-revoluta/Details|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|access-date=14 April 2020}} (confirmed 2017).{{cite web | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 22 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 24 January 2018}} ===Sago=== The [[pith]] contains edible [[starch]], and is used for making [[sago]]. Before use, the starch must be carefully washed to leach out [[toxin]]s contained in the pith. Extracting edible starch from the sago cycad requires special care due to the poisonous nature of cycads.{{cite web | last = Lafferty | first = Jamie | title=How a Plant Saved a Japanese Island|publisher=BBC|url=http://www.bbc.com/travel/story/20200106-how-a-plant-saved-a-japanese-island| date=2020-01-07}} Cycad sago is used for many of the same purposes as palm sago. Sago is extracted from the sago cycad by cutting the pith from the stem, root and seeds of the cycads, grinding the pith to a coarse flour and then washing it carefully and repeatedly to leach out the natural toxins. The starchy residue is then dried and cooked, producing a starch similar to palm sago/sabudana. The cycad seed contains cycasin toxin and should not be eaten as it is possible for [[cycasin]] toxin to survive the most vigorous of repeated washings. Cycasin toxin can cause [[ALS]], [[Parkinson's]], [[prostate cancer]] and [[fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma]].{{citation needed|date=March 2023}} ''[[Aulacaspis yasumatsui]]'' is a scale insect feeding on ''C. revoluta'', and unchecked is able to destroy the plant.Forrest W. Howard, Avas Hamon, Michael Mclaughlin, Thomas Weissling and Si-lin Yang "Aulacaspis yasumatsui (Hemiptera: Sternorrhyncha: Diaspididae), a Scale Insect Pest of Cycads Recently Introduced into Florida" ''The Florida Entomologist'' 1999; Vol. 82, No. 1, pages 14-27 [https://www.jstor.org/stable/3495833 article] == Chemistry == The hydro-alcoholic extract of leaves of ''C. revoluta'' shows the presence of alkaloids, steroids and tannins while the chloroform extract shows the presence of saponins, tannins and sugars.Leaves Of Cycas revoluta: Potent Antimicrobial And Antioxidant Agent. Manoj K Mourya, Archana Prakash, Ajay Swami, Gautam K Singh and Abhishek Mathur, World Journal of Science and Technology, 2011, Vol 1, No 10, pages 11-20 ([http://worldjournalofscience.com/index.php/wjst/article/viewFile/9793/4978 article]) Leaflets also contain [[biflavonoid]]s.{{cite journal | doi = 10.1055/s-0029-1240743 | volume=76 | title=Phytochemical Investigation of Cycas circinalis and Cycas revoluta Leaflets: Moderately Active Antibacterial Biflavonoids | year=2010 | journal=Planta Medica | pages=796–802 | last1 = Moawad | first1 = Abeer | issue=8 | pmid=20072955 | pmc=3711132 | bibcode=2010PlMed..76..796M }} [[Estragole]] is the primary volatile compound emitted from the male and female cones of ''C. revoluta''.{{cite journal | doi = 10.1007/s10265-006-0019-2 | volume=119 | title=Estragole (4-allylanisole) is the primary compound in volatiles emitted from the male and female cones of Cycas revoluta | year=2006 | journal=Journal of Plant Research | pages=671–676 | last1 = Azuma | first1 = Hiroshi | issue=6 | pmid=16932996 | bibcode=2006JPlR..119..671A }} == Toxicity == Cycad sago is extremely poisonous to animals (including humans) if ingested. Pets are at particular risk, since they seem to find the plant very palatable.''Suspected cycad (Cycas revoluta) intoxication in dogs'', Botha CJ, Naude TW, Swan GE, et al.| J S Afr Vet Assoc | 1991 Clinical symptoms of ingestion will develop within 12 hours, and may include [[vomiting]], [[diarrhea]], weakness, seizures, and liver failure or [[hepatotoxicity]] characterized by [[Jaundice|icterus]], [[cirrhosis]], and [[ascites]]. The pet may appear bruised, have nose bleeds (epistaxis), melena (blood in the stool), hematochezia (bloody straining), and hemarthrosis (blood in the joints).{{cite web |url=http://www.critterology.com/articles/cycas-revoluta-sago-palm-or-cycad-toxicity |first=Susan |last=Muller-Esneault |title=Cycas Revoluta: The Sago Palm, or Cycad Toxicity |year=2009 |publisher=Critterology.com |access-date=2009-05-12 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120605041620/http://www.critterology.com/articles/cycas-revoluta-sago-palm-or-cycad-toxicity |archive-date=2012-06-05 }} The ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center estimates a fatality rate of 50 to 75% when ingestion of the sago palm is involved. If any quantity of the plant is ingested, a poison control center or doctor should be contacted immediately. Effects of ingestion can include permanent internal damage and death. All parts of the plant are toxic; however, the seeds contain the highest level of the toxin [[cycasin]]. Cycasin causes gastrointestinal irritation, and in high enough doses, leads to liver failure.''Selected poisonous plant concerns small animals'', Knight MW, Dorman DC | Vet Med | 1997 | 92(3):260-272 Other toxins include [[Beta-methylamino L-alanine]], a [[neurotoxic]] [[amino acid]], and an unidentified toxin which has been observed to cause hindlimb paralysis in cattle.''Toxicology Brief: Cycad toxicosis in dogs'', Hany Youssef| Veterinary Medicine | May 1, 2008 | [http://veterinarymedicine.dvm360.com/vetmed/Toxicology+Brief/Toxicology-Brief-Cycad-toxicosis-in-dogs/ArticleStandard/Article/detail/516497?contextCategoryId=46382] == Gallery == File:Cycas revoluta female cone01.jpg|Female reproductive structure File:Cycas revoluta01.jpg File:Sago Palm.jpg File:Cycas revoluta1328A.JPG|Young leaves File:Cycas revoluta 020.jpg|Young leaflets curled back, "revoluta" File:Funchal, Monte -
